newsitem.title: CROATIA: FEATURE - Music pulls down walls between Serbia and Croatia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Music pulls down walls between Serbia and Croatia.

text.p: Despite Croatia's official vow to steer clear of anything from nearby Serbia, rock music seems to be re-tying knots that came undone in 1991 when Zagreb seceded from Serbian-dominated federal Yugoslavia.

Back in the 1980s, when Yugoslavia lived under the communist "Brotherhood and Unity" slogan, Croatian bands regularly toured other Yugoslav republics to popular acclaim. And the same went for rockers from Serbia.

But after 1991, when Croatia broke away from Yugoslavia after six months of war with the Serbian-led Yugoslav army, the Zagreb authorities set about eliminating all traces of Serbian culture in music, film, theatre and language.

Five years on, state media are still very careful about airing anything reminiscent of old Yugoslavia. They have gone as so far as banning from state-run television films and series starring Serbian or Croatian Serb actors.
However, Serbian rock music seems to be shaking off its political burden and making a slow if low-profile comeback.

Thousands of youngsters from Zagreb and other Croatian towns flocked to Slovenia, another ex-Yugoslav republic, in November when Serbian singer Djordje Balasevic staged two concerts in the capital Ljubljana.
Slovenia was the first to break away after a week of skirmishing with Yugoslav troops in 1991. It has remained open to all products, notably music, from former federal partners.
Many of the Croat visitors at Balasevic's Ljubljana concert carried banners saying "We love you". Some cried with emotion and lit candles throughout the concert.
Balasevic told them: "I am so glad to see you and hope to see you again in Zagreb". But in a subsequent interview for a Croatian daily, he admitted that the time was not yet ripe.
REAL NORMALISATION DISTANT, DESPITE RECOGNITION
Zagreb and Belgrade signed a mutual recognition accord last August, effectively ending the war. Despite diplomatic talk, real normalisation of relations still seems a way off.

When the state-run Croatia record company organised trips to a Balasevic concert in Ljubljana in 1995 and timidly announced the singer might perform in Zagreb in the future, it was flooded with criticism.
"Is this what we fought for -- to host singers from the country whose soldiers ravaged our homes?" wrote one woman in a letter to the independent Feral Tribune magazine.
"They would do better to stay where they are," she said.
Last month, the independent record company Dancing Bear was offered exclusive rights to distribute in Croatia albums of Serbia's two most prominent singers, a proposal unthinkable only a year before.
"We asked our retail sellers what they thought of it and about 75 percent replied it was still too early so we dropped it," a company spokesman told Reuters.
In another example of "music-turned-politics" the Croatian Music Union urged members to avoid one band after it transpired that it had played in Slovenia alongside a Serbian group.
TEENAGERS ARE NEW FANS
But the proscribed music has managed to recruit new followers -- teenagers -- most of whom only started listening to music after multinational Yugoslavia died.
An unprecedented pop cultural breakthrough occurred during a recent Croatian rock concert in Zagreb.
"The next song is by a friend of ours who is unfortunately no longer with us," one performer said, referring to a popular Serb singer who died of cancer last year.
After the first few bars, the unmistakably Serb song was met by wild applause from thousands of spectators.

Croat teenagers admit to indulging in pre-war Serbian music at home or at private parties. They have dug through their older brothers' record collections and re-emerged with forbidden fruit -- old Yugoslav music.
"Serbian music is the main item at parties. A lot of young people listen to it, especially those who find modern techno music boring," said 18-year-old Ivanka.

"I think listening to that music doesn't make me a lover of Serbia or old Yugoslavia," she said, but added that she would not go to a Serbian rock concert in Zagreb "out of respect for all the Croats who lost their lives" in the 1991 war.
In Serbia, sympathies for Croatian music extend even beyond furtive listening at parties.
"When you come to a Belgrade cafe you can easily mistake it for Zagreb -- Croatian music is played all the time," said Marina, 24, who recently visited the Serbian capital.
The Croatian band E.T. was the first to capture Belgraders by storm a few years ago. Their hit, "It's Only Midnight," topped the charts of private radio programmes for months.
"I am sure E.T. could sell out as many concerts in Belgrade as they want," said Belgrade rock star Momcilo Bajagic.
In a report from Belgrade, the Croatian weekly Nacional said its residents were dying to see Oliver Dragojevic, a Croatian singer who became popular long before the war broke out.

One promoter of Croatian music in Serbia is the daughter of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic. Marija Milosevic regularly plays Croatian songs on the air of her private "Kosava" radio, Nacional said.

Those who thrive most on reawakened interest in "music from beyond the barrier" are pirates on both sides. They smuggle or copy old and recent recordings and sell them to hungry listeners at or below street music stands.
